precepts.why:
“And Joseph was the governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land: and Joseph’s brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.” Our forefathers hated Joseph and sold him into slavery. He gained status in Egypt, Egypt got through the famine by his counsel, and now his brothers came to Egypt to buy food.

“And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.” If Joseph had been a German Jew, or from Holland, Ukraine or Poland, they would have known him: a white man in Egyptian clothes stands out among Egyptians, because the Egyptians are black. They could not recognize their brother because he was dressed in Egyptian garb, beard shaved, looking like an Egyptian. “for he spake unto them by an interpreter”: he acted the part, speaking Egyptian so they would not know him. Joseph passed for an African, a black man, just as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were dark ancestors.

Then Genesis 43:32, at the meal: “And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.” That is Jim Crow. The Hebrews sat over there and the Egyptians over here, because them sitting together was an abomination. Israel had its own land, Goshen, and Egypt was apart. It was still segregation, even though both were dark: same color, different nation.

The pictures shown from the history books said the same. The Egyptians are brown. The Israelites working in the granary under a taskmaster have afros. Pharaoh is black, and Tutankhamun is black. Nefertiti is black as hell, and the Nubians are black as hell. The sacrifice of Isaac in the mosaic of the Beth Alpha synagogue shows Abraham and Isaac as black. The sons of Ham, the Egyptians, Canaanites, Nubians and Libyans, are all dark; we fought the Canaanites in the land, and they are black too.

Moses passed for an Egyptian the same way. Jethro's daughters said, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. Moses married an Ethiopian woman, a daughter of Ham, and a Hamite would have known a white man was no Egyptian. Even Pharaoh's daughter knew the baby was a Hebrew only because he was circumcised, since both peoples were black.

precepts.point: This is a repeating thing in our history: when famine came, the fathers moved toward Egypt for sustenance and nourishment. There was a famine in Abram's days and he went down into Egypt, and another famine in Isaac's days, when the Lord told him not to go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
“And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.” This is a repeating thing in our history: when famine came, the fathers moved toward Egypt for sustenance and nourishment. There was a famine in Abram’s days and he went down into Egypt.

Now in Jacob’s days it is the same. Jacob heard there was corn in Egypt and sent his sons down thither to buy, “that we may live, and not die.” Egypt was where the bread was in the famine, for Abram and for Jacob.

precepts.text: In the famine of Isaac's days the Lord appeared unto him and said, go not down into Egypt; the pattern of famine and Egypt runs through the fathers.
precepts.point: This is a repeating thing in our history: when famine came, the fathers moved toward Egypt for sustenance and nourishment. There was a famine in Abram's days and he went down into Egypt, and another famine in Isaac's days, when the Lord told him not to go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
“And there was a famine in the land, beside the first famine that was in the days of Abraham.” In Isaac’s days the same pattern came round, and Isaac went toward Gerar; but this time “the Lord appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of.”

So the pattern of famine and Egypt runs through the fathers: Abram went down, Isaac was told not to go down, and now Jacob, seeing that there was corn in Egypt, sends his ten sons down to buy corn so the family may live and not die.

precepts.text: Rachel travailed in hard labour and died bearing Benjamin, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
precepts.point: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Rachel was barren for years; she brought forth only Joseph and Benjamin. With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was the last son Jacob had of his beloved wife, so he would not let him go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
Benjamin was Rachel’s son, and Rachel died bearing him. On the way to Ephrath “Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour”, and the midwife told her, “Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.” Then, “as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Ben–oni: but his father called him Benjamin. And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Beth–lehem.”

That is who Jacob would not send down with his brethren. Benjamin was the youngest boy, the son whose birth cost Rachel her life, and Jacob kept him back, “Lest peradventure mischief befall him”; peradventure means perhaps.

precepts.text: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Rachel was barren; Joseph and Benjamin were the only sons she brought forth.
precepts.point: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Rachel was barren for years; she brought forth only Joseph and Benjamin. With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was the last son Jacob had of his beloved wife, so he would not let him go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
“and he loved also Rachel more than Leah.” Jacob loved Rachel more, and served seven other years for her. “And when the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” Rachel was barren for years; she brought forth only two sons, Joseph and Benjamin.

With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was the last son Jacob had of his beloved wife. That is why he sent him not with his brethren, lest peradventure mischief befall him: he would not let the last son of Rachel go down.

precepts.text: The Canaanites saw the mourning and said, this is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; the twelve tribes were mistaken for Egyptians.
precepts.point: And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them. The sheaves that made obeisance to his sheaf were now his brethren bowing down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
When Jacob died and his sons carried him up to bury him, they mourned at the threshingfloor of Atad, and “when the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians.” The Canaanites saw the twelve tribes and took them all for Egyptians. Israel is black as night, just like the ancient Egyptians; all twelve tribes looked like the people of Egypt.

That is one reason Joseph’s brethren knew him not. He blended in among the Egyptians. Time had passed, they supposed he was dead or a slave, and they never expected their brother to be second in command over Egypt; and standing before them as an Egyptian ruler, speaking roughly, he looked like every other Egyptian in the land.

precepts.text: He made himself strange unto them and spake roughly; Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them.” From the first meeting, “Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.” He made himself strange on purpose, an Egyptian ruler asking a rough “Whence come ye?”

So when he finally says “I am Joseph”, they cannot answer him, troubled at his presence. They could not recognize their own brother. He was sold as a teenager and stood before them now a grown man in his years, and he had kept himself strange to them the whole time.

precepts.text: He spake unto them by an interpreter, though he understood every word.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And they knew not that Joseph understood them; for he spake unto them by an interpreter.” Joseph understood every word his brethren said, but he spoke to them through an interpreter as any Egyptian lord would. That was part of the strangeness he put on: a man who needs an interpreter for the tongue of Canaan could not be their brother.

No wonder they were troubled at his presence when he spoke to them plainly, “I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?”

precepts.text: Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him; an Israelite in Egyptian dress passed for an Egyptian.
precepts.point: Reuel the priest of Midian is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.

note.label: Exodus 2: The Birth of Moses

precepts.why:
Long before Moses, the same thing happened with Joseph: “And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them”. His own brothers stood before him and “Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.”

An Israelite in Egyptian dress passed for an Egyptian, even before his own brothers. So when the daughters of the priest of Midian called Moses an Egyptian, it was nothing new: Israel looked like the Egyptians, and Israel was always being mistaken for them.

Reuel, the priest of Midian who called Moses in to eat bread, is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.
